title: Week 6 · Lesson 17: Gastrointestinal Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 6 — Lesson 17: Gastrointestinal Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal

Use anatomy, mucosal injury, inflammation, bleeding physiology, and risk stratification to approach reflux, peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease, and functional bowel symptoms—while recognizing abdominal or bleeding presentations that are unsafe for outpatient management.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain GERD, peptic ulcer disease, and upper GI bleeding through barrier failure and mucosal injury.
  • Distinguish inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) using mechanism and alarm features.
  • Use stool appearance, hemodynamics, and risk factors to reason through GI bleeding.
  • Build a focused differential for abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and chronic diarrhea.
  • Recognize when urgent imaging, endoscopy, specialty referral, or emergency care is needed.

Part 1 — Abdominal complaints need a safety screen first

Abdominal pain, reflux, diarrhea, nausea, and altered bowel habits are common in primary care, but the first task is not to assign a benign label. Ask about onset, location, migration, severity, vomiting, fever, bowel changes, bleeding, weight loss, pregnancy possibility, medication use, alcohol, prior surgery, immune status, and cardiopulmonary symptoms.

Peritoneal signs, severe or worsening pain, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, syncope, hypotension, fever with toxicity, jaundice, rigid abdomen, altered mentation, or inability to maintain hydration require urgent/emergency assessment. Abdominal pain can be a manifestation of GI disease, ACS, aortic pathology, metabolic disease, infection, or pregnancy-related emergency.

Part 2 — GERD: barrier failure, not just “too much acid”

The lower esophageal sphincter and diaphragm normally limit reflux. GERD develops when this barrier is weak or relaxes inappropriately, allowing gastric contents to reach the esophagus. Typical symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation, often affected by meals or position.

Do not automatically call chest discomfort “reflux.” Exertional pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, radiation, syncope, or cardiovascular risk can indicate ischemia. Dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, bleeding, weight loss, or anemia are alarm features that warrant further evaluation rather than repeated empiric therapy alone.

Part 3 — Peptic ulcer disease: mucosal defense versus injury

Peptic ulcers occur when mucosal defense is overwhelmed by injurious factors. The most common causes are H. pylori infection and NSAID exposure. NSAIDs reduce protective prostaglandin-mediated mucosal defenses, making injury and bleeding more likely. Upper abdominal burning or discomfort may occur, but symptoms do not reliably predict complication risk.

Ulcer complications include bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction. Sudden severe persistent abdominal pain, guarding/rigidity, hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, dizziness, or shock are not outpatient ulcer follow-up issues.

Part 4 — GI bleeding: localize, quantify, stabilize

Black tarry stool (melena) often suggests upper GI bleeding, while bright red blood per rectum can arise from lower bleeding but may also occur with brisk upper bleeding. Coffee-ground emesis or hematemesis indicates upper GI bleeding. Stool appearance helps localize but does not establish severity.

Assess circulation early: heart rate, blood pressure, orthostasis, perfusion, mental status, urine output, anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure, and signs of ongoing loss. Tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, pallor, confusion, or shock require emergency care. A single hemoglobin value early in acute bleeding does not replace clinical assessment.

Part 5 — IBD: chronic immune-mediated intestinal inflammation

IBD includes ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn disease. UC typically involves continuous colonic mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum; Crohn disease can involve any part of the GI tract, often with patchy transmural inflammation. Both can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, urgency, rectal bleeding, weight loss, fatigue, anemia, and extraintestinal manifestations.

In suspected IBD, exclude infectious causes and characterize severity and extent. Bloody diarrhea, high stool frequency/urgency, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, fever, and family history are not explained safely by IBS without appropriate evaluation. Severe colitis with systemic toxicity, dehydration, abdominal distention, or significant bleeding needs urgent escalation.

Part 6 — IBS: functional symptoms after red flags are considered

IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction, often characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with defecation and altered stool form/frequency. It does not cause the mucosal inflammation, progressive anemia, GI bleeding, nocturnal systemic symptoms, or unintentional weight loss expected with structural/inflammatory disease.

IBS is a positive clinical diagnosis in an appropriate patient, not a dismissal. Before applying it, assess alarm features: GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, unexplained weight loss, persistent nocturnal symptoms, fever, family history of colorectal cancer/IBD, new onset at older age, or abnormal examination/laboratory findings.

Part 7 — Chronic diarrhea and differential diagnosis

Chronic diarrhea may be inflammatory, infectious, malabsorptive, medication-related, endocrine-related, functional, or due to IBD, celiac disease, bile-acid disorders, microscopic colitis, or malignancy. Stool frequency alone is not enough: distinguish watery, fatty, and inflammatory/bloody patterns; assess nocturnal symptoms, travel, antibiotics, immune status, diet, medication exposure, hydration, and weight change.

Use targeted testing to answer a clinical question. Stool studies, blood counts, metabolic tests, inflammatory markers, and endoscopic evaluation are selected according to the pattern and risk—not ordered identically for every patient.

Part 8 — Colorectal risk and occult disease

Persistent change in bowel habits, blood in stool, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, unintentional weight loss, or persistent abdominal pain requires assessment for structural disease, including colorectal cancer, as clinically appropriate. Many colorectal cancers or polyps do not cause early symptoms; prevention and screening remain distinct from evaluating a symptomatic patient.

Case 1 — “Indigestion” with cardiac risk

A 62-year-old with diabetes and hypertension reports new pressure-like epigastric discomfort with exertion, nausea, and dyspnea. GERD is possible, but cardiac ischemia remains a high-risk alternative. The FNP-level decision is emergency cardiovascular evaluation rather than assuming a GI source from the word “indigestion.”

Case 2 — Melena and dizziness

A patient using NSAIDs reports black stools, lightheadedness, tachycardia, and weakness. The chain is possible NSAID-related mucosal injury → ulcer → upper GI bleeding → reduced circulating volume/oxygen delivery. This requires emergency assessment.

Case 3 — Chronic bloody diarrhea

A young adult reports weeks of urgent bloody diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, and nocturnal stools. This is not a typical IBS pattern. Consider IBD and infection; evaluate severity, anemia, hydration, inflammatory features, and need for GI referral or emergency care.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Screen for instability and surgical/bleeding red flags before labeling symptoms as benign.
  2. For reflux/ulcer symptoms, consider mucosal injury, medication exposure, H. pylori risk, and cardiopulmonary mimics.
  3. For bleeding, assess hemodynamics and ongoing loss—not stool appearance alone.
  4. For bowel symptoms, distinguish inflammatory/structural disease from functional IBS using alarm features.
  5. Use targeted diagnostics and early referral for significant bleeding, suspected IBD, alarm features, or unresolved iron-deficiency anemia.

High-Yield Summary

GERD: LES/diaphragm barrier failure; do not mistake cardiac ischemia for reflux.
PUD: H. pylori or NSAIDs commonly disrupt mucosal defense; bleeding/perforation are emergencies.
GI bleeding: melena, hematemesis, coffee grounds, or hematochezia require severity/hemodynamic assessment.
IBD: immune-mediated inflammation with bleeding, urgency, anemia, weight loss, and systemic features.
IBS: functional disorder; does not explain alarm features such as bleeding, anemia, weight loss, or nocturnal systemic symptoms.
Emergency red flags: shock, syncope, active bleeding, severe persistent/peritoneal pain, dehydration, systemic toxicity, or possible ACS.
